title: Diwali flight fares soar: Delhi-Patna hits ₹12,500 as demand spikes
excerpt: Regional routes are seeing fares triple ahead of the November 8 festival, with Kolkata-Deoghar up 340 percent and last-minute Delhi-Patna tickets crossing ₹13,500. The DGCA has asked airlines to add over 1,760 flights to check the surge.
body:
• One-way economy fares on some regional routes have tripled ahead of Diwali 2026, with Kolkata-Deoghar jumping about 340 percent to roughly ₹12,500 from a usual ₹2,800.
  • Delhi-Patna fares have crossed ₹12,500 on peak festive dates, with last-minute direct tickets going beyond ₹13,500, according to Moneycontrol data cited by Curly Tales.
  • The DGCA has intervened, asking IndiGo, Air India and SpiceJet to add more than 1,760 flights across October and November to check fare spikes.
  • Aviation Turbine Fuel rose 5.46 percent on September 1 — the second straight monthly increase — adding to airline cost pressure.

With Diwali approaching on November 8, domestic airfares across India are climbing sharply, and some routes are already selling at two to three times their normal prices. The steepest increases are on sectors connecting major cities with smaller regional airports, where limited direct flight options give airlines room to push fares far higher.

Delhi-Patna non-stop economy fares that usually cost ₹3,500 to ₹4,500 have crossed ₹12,500 on peak dates, with last-minute direct tickets going beyond ₹13,500, according to Moneycontrol figures cited by Curly Tales. The Kolkata-Deoghar sector, usually a ₹2,800 hop, has climbed to approximately ₹12,500 during the Durga Puja travel period — an increase of around 340 percent. Delhi-Agatti fares jumped nearly 194 percent, from ₹8,500 to about ₹25,000, and Bengaluru-Jharsuguda rose from roughly ₹4,200 to ₹16,200.

Context & Background

The surge follows a familiar pattern: Diwali is the peak of India's festive travel season, and millions fly home in the weeks around the festival. This year the five-day festival runs from November 6 to 10, with Lakshmi Puja falling on Sunday, November 8. Airlines know demand will come regardless of price, and their dynamic pricing systems respond accordingly — seats released later sell at higher fares.

Regulators stepped in this past weekend. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation said in a statement on Saturday that it had taken up the fare issue with carriers after reviewing airfare patterns on major domestic routes, instructing airlines to expand capacity and keep prices reasonable. In response, IndiGo — which controls about 64 percent of the domestic market — will add around 730 flights across 42 routes, Air India and Air India Express will deploy nearly 486 flights on 20 sectors, and SpiceJet will introduce about 546 flights across 38 routes through October and November.

Cost pressures are also running against passengers. Domestic Aviation Turbine Fuel prices rose 5.46 percent to ₹121.28 per litre on September 1 — the second straight monthly increase. Fuel accounts for 35 to 40 percent of airline operating costs, and fleet delivery delays and engine maintenance have further squeezed available capacity.

"The DGCA will maintain rigorous oversight of airline fares and flight capacities to protect passengers' interests during the festive season."

— Directorate General of Civil Aviation

Impact & Analysis

The pain is concentrated on regional routes. Mumbai-Bareilly fares have risen from a usual ₹4,500 to more than ₹15,000, and Mumbai-Kolkata direct economy tickets that normally cost ₹5,000 to ₹6,500 are selling for ₹11,500 to ₹14,200 during the Durga Puja period. On major metro-to-metro routes, by contrast, competition is keeping increases moderate: Delhi-Kolkata fares crossed ₹12,300 from an off-peak ₹4,800, Delhi-Bengaluru tickets reached about ₹10,000, and Delhi-Mumbai is hovering around ₹7,000.

This gap is structural. Metro routes have several carriers competing; regional sectors often have one or two operators with limited daily frequencies. When festive demand arrives, inventory on those thin routes disappears within days, and pricing algorithms push what remains to peak fares. The DGCA's added capacity may help, but only if it lands on the regional routes where demand is spiking — exactly where aircraft availability is thinnest.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs planning a Diwali trip home, the domestic leg is usually priced last. International tickets are booked months ahead; the connecting domestic flight from Delhi, Mumbai or Kolkata is often booked late — exactly when fares peak. Lock in domestic tickets now, and consider flexible routing: a metro flight plus a train connection can cost far less than a last-minute direct regional ticket.

What's Next

If you haven't booked yet: book 60 to 90 days ahead, consider flying on the actual festival day when demand dips, and know Tuesdays and Wednesdays are generally cheapest. Watch the DGCA's fare monitoring through October — but don't count on it. Seats on the busiest regional routes will not get cheaper between now and November 8.
